items.stem: Which of these is an effect a force can have on an object?
options: Changing its density permanently by heating
items.answer: Changing its shape
items.markingKey: Forces can change speed, direction or shape (size).

items.stem: Describe how to obtain a load-extension graph for a spring.
items.answer: Clamp the spring next to a vertical metre rule; record the unloaded length; add masses one at a time, recording the length each time; extension = length − original length; plot load against extension.
items.markingKey: set-up with ruler and pointer [1]; add loads and record length [1]; calculate extension and plot [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how a load-extension graph shows that a spring obeys Hooke’s law.
items.answer: The graph is a straight line through the origin, showing extension is directly proportional to load.
items.markingKey: straight line [1]; through origin [1] [2]

items.stem: Yusuf loads a spring and records: load/N = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; length/cm = 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11.8. Calculate the extension for a load of 2 N.
items.answer: 2 cm
items.markingKey: extension = 7 − 5 = 2 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Lina loads a spring and records: load/N = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; length/cm = 3, 3.8, 4.6, 5.4, 6.2, 7.6, 9.4. Calculate the extension for each load up to 3 N and state whether the spring obeys Hooke’s law over this range, giving a reason.
items.answer: 0, 0.8, 1.6, 2.4 cm; yes: extension is proportional to load (0.8 cm per N).
items.markingKey: extensions correct [1]; equal increases of 0.8 cm per N / proportional [1]; conclusion [1] [3]

items.stem: A student hangs loads on a spring of original length 2 cm: load/N 0–6 in 1 N steps; length/cm = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 14, 16.4. (a) Describe the shape of the load-extension graph. (b) State two safety precautions.
items.answer: (a) Straight line through the origin up to 4 N, then curving (extension increasing faster). (b) Wear eye protection; place a tray/soft surface under the masses; do not overload.
items.markingKey: (a) straight through origin [1]; curves after limit [1] [2] (b) Wear eye protection [1]; place a tray/soft surface under the masses, do not overload [1] [2]

items.stem: The extension of a spring is …
options: its stretched length minus its original length
the load divided by its length
items.answer: its stretched length minus its original length
items.markingKey: extension = new length − original (unloaded) length.

items.stem: Explain why a student should check the spring’s length after removing the loads.
items.answer: If the length has not returned to the original, the spring has been stretched beyond its elastic limit and permanently deformed.
items.markingKey: check return to original length [1]; elastic limit / permanent deformation [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how the load-extension graph for a rubber band differs from that for a steel spring.
items.answer: The rubber band’s graph is curved (not proportional) from early on, and it does not obey Hooke’s law; the spring is straight up to its limit of proportionality.
items.markingKey: rubber curved / non-linear [1]; spring straight to limit [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a pointer and eye-level reading are used when measuring the length of a loaded spring.
items.answer: A pointer fixed to the bottom of the spring gives a definite mark on the scale; reading at eye level avoids parallax error.
items.markingKey: pointer [1]; parallax [1] [2]

items.stem: Ana loads a spring and records: load/N = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; length/cm = 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14.8. Calculate the extension for a load of 2 N.
items.answer: 2 cm
items.markingKey: extension = 10 − 8 = 2 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Hana loads a spring and records: load/N = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; length/cm = 6, 6.8, 7.6, 8.4, 9.2, 10.5, 12.1. Calculate the extension for each load up to 3 N and state whether the spring obeys Hooke’s law over this range, giving a reason.
items.answer: 0, 0.8, 1.6, 2.4 cm; yes: extension is proportional to load (0.8 cm per N).
items.markingKey: extensions correct [1]; equal increases of 0.8 cm per N / proportional [1]; conclusion [1] [3]

items.stem: What is the unit of the spring constant?
items.answer: N/m
items.markingKey: k = F/x: newtons per metre.

items.stem: A spring with k = 50 N/m is stretched by 0.10 m. What force is needed?
Two springs are tested. Spring P extends 4 cm and spring Q extends 8 cm under the same load. Explain which has the larger spring constant.
items.answer: P: k = F/x, so for the same force a smaller extension means a larger k (stiffer).
items.markingKey: P [1]; k = F/x with smaller x [1] [2]

items.stem: A force of 40 N stretches a door-closer spring by 0.08 m. Calculate the spring constant.
items.markingKey: k = F/x = 40/0.08 = 500 N/m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Two springs A (k = 40 N/m) and B (k = 100 N/m) are tested by Hana. (a) Calculate the extension of B for the same load. (b) Suggest which spring would be better for a newton meter that must measure forces up to 1 N precisely, and why.
items.answer: (a) 0.02 m (b) A: lower k gives larger extension per newton, so readings are more precise.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.02 m [1] (b) A [1]; lower k gives larger extension per newton, so readings are more precise [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the spring constant can only be calculated from the straight part of a load-extension graph.
items.answer: Only there is extension proportional to load, so F/x is constant; beyond the limit of proportionality F/x changes.
items.markingKey: proportional region [1]; F/x not constant beyond [1] [2]

items.stem: A force of 100 N stretches a car suspension spring by 0.002 m. Calculate the spring constant.
items.markingKey: k = F/x = 100/0.002 = 50 000 N/m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A mass of 2.45 kg hung on a door-closer spring stretches it by 12 cm (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) Calculate the weight of the mass. (b) Calculate the spring constant. (c) Calculate the extension for a load of 12 N, assuming the limit of proportionality is not reached.
items.markingKey: (a) W = mg = 24 N [1] (b) k = 24/0.12 = 200 N/m [2] (c) x = F/k = 6 cm [1]; assumption stated (Hooke’s law / within limit) [1] [5]

items.stem: Two springs A (k = 50 N/m) and B (k = 20 N/m) are tested by Mei. (a) Describe how the load-extension graphs of the two springs would differ. (b) Suggest which spring would be better for a newton meter that must measure forces up to 1 N precisely, and why.
items.answer: (a) Both straight lines through the origin (in the linear region); the stiffer spring has the steeper line if load is on the y-axis. (b) B: lower k gives larger extension per newton, so readings are more precise.
items.markingKey: (a) Both straight lines through the origin (in the linear region) [1]; the stiffer spring has the steeper line if load is on the y-axis [1] [2] (b) B [1]; lower k gives larger extension per newton, so readings are more precise [1] [2]

items.stem: Which equation defines pressure?
items.answer: pressure = force ÷ area
items.markingKey: p = F/A.

items.stem: Explain why a drawing pin has a broad head and a sharp point.
items.answer: The sharp point has a tiny area so the pressure is large enough to pierce the board; the broad head spreads the force over a large area so the pressure on the thumb is small.
items.markingKey: point small area → high pressure [1]; head large area → low pressure on thumb [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why tractors have wide tyres.
items.answer: Wide tyres spread the weight over a larger area, reducing the pressure on soft ground so the tractor does not sink.
items.markingKey: larger area [1]; smaller pressure, less sinking [1] [2]

items.stem: A water tank exerts a force of 100 N on an area of 0.02 m². Work out the pressure.
items.markingKey: p = F/A = 100/0.02 = 5000 Pa. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An elephant of weight 40000 N stands on four feet, each of area 40 cm × 40 cm. Calculate the pressure on the ground in Pa.

A car tyre presses on the road with a force of 3000 N over a contact patch 20 cm × 30 cm. (a) Calculate the total contact area in m². (b) Calculate the pressure. (c) Calculate the pressure if the contact area is halved and explain the effect on soft ground.
items.answer: (a) 0.06 m² (b) 50 000 Pa (c) 100 000 Pa: doubled pressure, so it sinks further into soft ground.

items.stem: A machine of mass 1000 kg is to be placed on a floor in Dhaka that can safely withstand a pressure of 8000 Pa. Its base has an area of 0.5 m² (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) Calculate the weight of the machine. (b) Calculate the minimum area of base needed. (c) Suggest how this area could be achieved.
items.answer: (a) 9800 N (b) 1.23 m² (c) Stand the machine on a wide metal plate / board to spread its weight.
items.markingKey: (a) 9800 N [1] (b) A = F/p = 9800/8000 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.23 m² with unit [1] [2] (c) Stand the machine on a wide metal plate / board to spread its weight [1]

items.stem: A machine of mass 1200 kg is to be placed on a floor in Dhaka that can safely withstand a pressure of 5000 Pa. Its base has an area of 0.25 m² (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) Calculate the weight of the machine. (b) Calculate the pressure under the base. (c) State whether the floor is safe and justify your answer. (d) Suggest how this area could be achieved.
items.answer: (a) 11 800 N (b) 47 000 Pa (c) Safe only if a larger base is used: 47 000 Pa > 5000 Pa. (d) Stand the machine on a wide metal plate / board to spread its weight.
items.markingKey: (a) 11 800 N [1] (b) p = F/A (method/substitution) [1]; answer 47 000 Pa with unit [1] [2] (c) Safe only if a larger base is used: 47 000 Pa > 5000 Pa [1] (d) Stand the machine on a wide metal plate / board to spread its weight [1]

items.stem: What is the unit of pressure?
items.answer: pascal (Pa)
items.markingKey: 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

items.stem: Explain why a woman in stiletto heels can damage a wooden floor that an elephant walking on it would not.
items.answer: The heel area is tiny so the pressure under it can be very large even though her weight is much smaller; the elephant’s weight is spread over large feet.
items.markingKey: small area high pressure [1]; comparison with large area [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a brick exerts different pressures on the ground depending on which face it rests on, although its weight is the same.
items.answer: Pressure = weight ÷ area of contact; different faces have different areas, so the smallest face gives the largest pressure.
items.markingKey: p = F/A [1]; smallest area gives largest pressure [1] [2]

items.stem: An engineer designs the base of a heavy machine. The contact area is multiplied by 5 while the force stays the same. Explain how the pressure changes.
items.answer: The pressure falls to one fifth.
items.markingKey: Using p = F/A: pressure ∝ contact area^-1.00; factor = 5.00^-1.00 = 0.200. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A stack of books exerts a force of 750 N on an area of 0.02 m². Work out the pressure.
items.markingKey: p = F/A = 750/0.02 = 37 500 Pa. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A table leg exerts a force of 100 N on an area of 0.05 m². Determine the pressure.
items.markingKey: p = F/A = 100/0.05 = 2000 Pa. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A brick of weight 40 N rests on a face measuring 6 cm × 4 cm. Calculate the pressure on the ground in Pa.

A machine of mass 800 kg is to be placed on a floor in Cairo that can safely withstand a pressure of 15000 Pa. Its base has an area of 0.5 m² (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) State whether the floor is safe and justify your answer. (b) Calculate the minimum area of base needed. (c) Suggest how this area could be achieved.
items.answer: (a) Safe only if a larger base is used: 15 700 Pa > 15000 Pa. (b) 0.523 m² (c) Stand the machine on a wide metal plate / board to spread its weight.
items.markingKey: (a) Safe only if a larger base is used: 15 700 Pa > 15000 Pa [1] (b) A = F/p = 7840/15000 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.523 m² with unit [1] [2] (c) Stand the machine on a wide metal plate / board to spread its weight [1]

items.stem: A machine of mass 1000 kg is to be placed on a floor in Madrid that can safely withstand a pressure of 5000 Pa. Its base has an area of 0.4 m² (g = 9.8 N/kg). (a) Calculate the weight of the machine. (b) State whether the floor is safe and justify your answer. (c) Calculate the minimum area of base needed. (d) Suggest how this area could be achieved.
items.answer: (a) 9800 N (b) Safe only if a larger base is used: 24 500 Pa > 5000 Pa. (c) 1.96 m² (d) Stand the machine on a wide metal plate / board to spread its weight.
items.markingKey: (a) 9800 N [1] (b) Safe only if a larger base is used: 24 500 Pa > 5000 Pa [1] (c) A = F/p = 9800/5000 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.96 m² with unit [1] [2] (d) Stand the machine on a wide metal plate / board to spread its weight [1]

items.stem: Pressure in a liquid increases with …
options: depth and density of the liquid
items.answer: depth and density of the liquid
items.markingKey: Δp = ρgΔh.

items.stem: Water spurts from holes at different heights in the side of a tall container. Explain why water from the lowest hole travels furthest.
items.answer: The lowest hole is deepest, so the pressure there is greatest and water is pushed out fastest.
items.markingKey: deepest point [1]; greatest pressure [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a diver’s ears hurt more at 10 m depth than at 2 m.
items.answer: Pressure increases with depth (Δp = ρgh); at 10 m the extra pressure on the eardrum is five times larger.
items.markingKey: pressure increases with depth [1]; quantitative or force on eardrum [1] [2]

items.stem: A point at the bottom of a mercury column in a barometer tube is 0.1 m below the surface of mercury (density 13 600 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg). Work out the pressure due to the liquid.
items.markingKey: Δp = ρgΔh = 13600 × 9.8 × 0.1 = 13 300 Pa. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A point at the bottom of a reservoir is 12 m below the surface of fresh water (density 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg). Calculate the pressure due to the liquid in kPa.
items.answer: 118 kPa

items.stem: A window of area 0.05 m² is 1.2 m below the surface of fresh water (density 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg; atmospheric pressure = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa). (a) Calculate the pressure due to the liquid. (b) Calculate the total pressure on the window. (c) Calculate the force on the window due to the total pressure.

A remotely operated camera is lowered 10 m into the sea (density 1030 kg/m³). Atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa; g = 9.8 N/kg. (a) Calculate the force from the total pressure on a viewing window of area 0.015 m². (b) Calculate the depth at which the pressure due to the water equals atmospheric pressure.
items.markingKey: (a) F = pA (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3010 N with unit [1] [2] (b) h = p/(ρg) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 9.91 m with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A remotely operated camera is lowered 15 m into the sea (density 1030 kg/m³). Atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa; g = 9.8 N/kg. (a) Calculate the force from the total pressure on a viewing window of area 0.015 m². (b) Explain why the pressure acts on the mask from all directions. (c) Calculate the depth at which the pressure due to the water equals atmospheric pressure.
items.answer: (a) 3770 N (b) Pressure in a fluid at a point acts equally in all directions. (c) 9.91 m
items.markingKey: (a) F = pA (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3770 N with unit [1] [2] (b) Pressure in a fluid at a point acts equally in all directions [1] (c) h = p/(ρg) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 9.91 m with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: At a given depth, the pressure in a liquid acts …
items.answer: equally in all directions
items.markingKey: Liquid pressure acts in all directions at a point.

items.stem: Explain why the pressure at the bottom of a narrow tube of water 0.5 m tall is the same as at the bottom of a wide tank of water 0.5 m deep.
items.answer: Liquid pressure depends only on depth, density and g, not on the width or volume of the container.
items.markingKey: depends on ρ, g, h only [1]; not area/volume [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the total pressure on a diver is greater than ρgh.
items.answer: Atmospheric pressure also acts on the water surface, so total pressure = atmospheric pressure + ρgh.
items.markingKey: atmospheric pressure adds [1]; p = p_atm + ρgh [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a diver’s ears hurt more at 10 m depth than at 2 m. (b) Explain why the total pressure on a diver is greater than ρgh.
items.answer: (a) Pressure increases with depth (Δp = ρgh); at 10 m the extra pressure on the eardrum is five times larger. (b) Atmospheric pressure also acts on the water surface, so total pressure = atmospheric pressure + ρgh.
items.markingKey: (a) pressure increases with depth [1]; quantitative or force on eardrum [1] [2] (b) atmospheric pressure adds [1]; p = p_atm + ρgh [1] [2]

items.stem: At a depth of 2 m in oil (density 800 kg/m³), the pressure due to the liquid is p. Calculate the depth in sea water (density 1030 kg/m³) at which the liquid pressure is also p.
At a depth of 4 m in brine (density 1200 kg/m³), the pressure due to the liquid is p. Calculate the depth in fresh water (density 1000 kg/m³) at which the liquid pressure is also p.
The pressure due to mercury (density 13 600 kg/m³) at the bottom of a mercury column in a barometer tube is 101 000 Pa (g = 9.8 N/kg). Calculate the depth.

A remotely operated camera is lowered 30 m into the sea (density 1030 kg/m³). Atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa; g = 9.8 N/kg. (a) Calculate the pressure due to the water at this depth. (b) Calculate the force from the total pressure on a viewing window of area 0.015 m².
items.markingKey: (a) ρgh (method/substitution) [1]; answer 303 000 Pa with unit [1] [2] (b) F = pA (method/substitution) [1]; answer 6040 N with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A diver descends to 15 m in sea water (density 1030 kg/m³) near Dubai. Atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa; g = 9.8 N/kg. (a) Calculate the total pressure. (b) Calculate the force from the total pressure on a viewing window of area 0.015 m². (c) Explain why the pressure acts on the mask from all directions. (d) Calculate the depth at which the pressure due to the water equals atmospheric pressure.
items.answer: (a) 251 000 Pa (b) 3770 N (c) Pressure in a fluid at a point acts equally in all directions. (d) 9.91 m
items.markingKey: (a) 251 000 Pa [1] (b) F = pA (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3770 N with unit [1] [2] (c) Pressure in a fluid at a point acts equally in all directions [1] (d) h = p/(ρg) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 9.91 m with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Hooke’s law states that, up to the limit of proportionality, …
options: the extension is directly proportional to the load
the extension is inversely proportional to the load
the length is proportional to the load
items.answer: the extension is directly proportional to the load
items.markingKey: F ∝ x for a spring obeying Hooke’s law.

items.stem: A spring has an unloaded length of 5 cm and is 6 cm long with a load of 2 N. Freya predicts that a 4 N load will make the spring 12 cm long. Explain the mistake and give the correct prediction (assume Hooke’s law applies).
items.answer: Freya doubled the length instead of the extension. Extension = 1 cm, so for 4 N it is 2 cm and the length is 7 cm.
items.markingKey: extension (not length) ∝ load [1]; correct extension [1]; correct length [1] [3]

items.stem: Lucas loads a spring and records: load/N = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; length/cm = 8, 8.5, 9, 9.5, 10, 10.9, 11.8. Determine the extension for a load of 1 N.
items.answer: 0.5 cm
items.markingKey: extension = 8.5 − 8 = 0.5 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A student hangs loads on a spring of original length 4 cm: load/N 0–6 in 1 N steps; length/cm = 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 17.2. (a) Describe the shape of the load-extension graph. (b) Describe how the student could test whether the spring has gone beyond its elastic limit.
items.answer: (a) Straight line through the origin up to 5 N, then curving (extension increasing faster). (b) Remove all loads and see whether the spring returns to its original length.
items.markingKey: (a) straight through origin [1]; curves after limit [1] [2] (b) Remove all loads and see whether the spring returns to its original length (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2]

items.stem: A student hangs loads on a spring of original length 4 cm: load/N 0–6 in 1 N steps; length/cm = 4, 6.5, 9, 11.5, 14, 19, 23. (a) Calculate the extension for a load of 3 N. (b) Describe the shape of the load-extension graph. (c) Calculate the spring constant in N/m using the straight part. (d) State the load at the limit of proportionality.
items.answer: (a) 7.5 cm (b) Straight line through the origin up to 4 N, then curving (extension increasing faster). (c) 40 N/m (d) 4 N (approximately)
items.markingKey: (a) 7.5 cm [1] (b) straight through origin [1]; curves after limit [1] [2] (c) k = F/x = 1 N/0.025 m (method/substitution) [1]; answer 40 N/m with unit [1] [2] (d) 4 N (approximately) [1]

items.stem: A stiffer spring has …
options: a larger extension for the same load
items.answer: a larger spring constant
items.markingKey: Larger k: more force per metre of extension.

items.stem: Explain why the extension must be in metres when calculating k in N/m.
items.answer: The unit N/m requires force in newtons divided by extension in metres; using cm would give a value 100 times too small.
items.markingKey: unit consistency [1]; factor of 100 [1] [2]

items.stem: A trampoline spring has a spring constant of 2000 N/m and is stretched by 0.01 m. Work out the force needed.
items.markingKey: F = kx = 2000 × 0.01 = 20 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A force of 100 N acts on an area of 2 m². What is the pressure? (b) Why is a sharp knife better for cutting than a blunt one?
items.answer: (a) 50 Pa (b) The small area of the blade gives a large pressure
items.markingKey: (a) p = 100/2 = 50 Pa. (b) Same force on smaller area → larger pressure.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a woman in stiletto heels can damage a wooden floor that an elephant walking on it would not. (b) Explain why a drawing pin has a broad head and a sharp point.
items.answer: (a) The heel area is tiny so the pressure under it can be very large even though her weight is much smaller; the elephant’s weight is spread over large feet. items.answer: The pressure due to the liquid becomes a quarter.
items.markingKey: Using Δp = ρgΔh: pressure due to the liquid ∝ density of the liquid; factor = 0.250 = 0.250. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.markingKey: Δp = ρgΔh = 13600 × 9.8 × 0.76 = 101 000 Pa. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

(b) Calculate the force from the total pressure on a viewing window of area 0.015 m². (c) Explain why the pressure acts on the mask from all directions.

items.markingKey: (a) ρgh (method/substitution) [1]; answer 505 000 Pa with unit [1] [2] (b) F = pA (method/substitution) [1]; answer 9070 N with unit [1] [2] (c) Pressure in a fluid at a point acts equally in all directions [1]

items.stem: On a load-extension graph, where does the limit of proportionality occur?
options: Where the straight line starts to curve
items.answer: Where the straight line starts to curve
items.markingKey: Beyond this point extension is no longer proportional to load.

items.stem: A spring has an unloaded length of 2 cm and is 8 cm long with a load of 3 N. Aisha predicts that a 6 N load will make the spring 16 cm long. Explain the mistake and give the correct prediction (assume Hooke’s law applies).
items.answer: Aisha doubled the length instead of the extension. Extension = 6 cm, so for 6 N it is 12 cm and the length is 14 cm.
items.markingKey: extension (not length) ∝ load [1]; correct extension [1]; correct length [1] [3]

items.stem: Ines loads a spring and records: load/N = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; length/cm = 8, 8.5, 9, 9.5, 10, 10.5, 11.3. Determine the extension for a load of 3 N.
items.answer: 1.5 cm
items.markingKey: extension = 9.5 − 8 = 1.5 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A student hangs loads on a spring of original length 4 cm: load/N 0–6 in 1 N steps; length/cm = 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 20. (a) Calculate the extension for a load of 3 N. (b) State the load at the limit of proportionality. (c) Describe how the student could test whether the spring has gone beyond its elastic limit.
items.answer: (a) 6 cm (b) 4 N (approximately) (c) Remove all loads and see whether the spring returns to its original length.

items.stem: A student hangs loads on a spring of original length 4 cm: load/N 0–6 in 1 N steps; length/cm = 4, 6.5, 9, 11.5, 14, 16.5, 21.5. items.stem: A newton meter spring is used within its limit of proportionality. The load is tripled. Explain how the extension changes.
items.answer: The extension triples.

items.stem: A force of 0.8 N stretches a spring in a ballpoint pen by 0.002 m. Calculate the spring constant.
items.markingKey: k = F/x = 0.8/0.002 = 400 N/m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Why is a sharp knife better for cutting than a blunt one? (b) A force of 100 N acts on an area of 2 m². What is the pressure?
items.answer: (a) The small area of the blade gives a large pressure (b) 50 Pa
items.markingKey: (a) Same force on smaller area → larger pressure. (b) p = 100/2 = 50 Pa.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why a woman in stiletto heels can damage a wooden floor that an elephant walking on it would not. (b) Explain why a brick exerts different pressures on the ground depending on which face it rests on, although its weight is the same.
items.answer: (a) The heel area is tiny so the pressure under it can be very large even though her weight is much smaller; the elephant’s weight is spread over large feet. (b) Pressure = weight ÷ area of contact; different faces have different areas, so the smallest face gives the largest pressure.
items.markingKey: (a) small area high pressure [1]; comparison with large area [1] [2] (b) p = F/A [1]; smallest area gives largest pressure [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why tractors have wide tyres. (b) Explain why a drawing pin has a broad head and a sharp point.
items.answer: (a) Wide tyres spread the weight over a larger area, reducing the pressure on soft ground so the tractor does not sink. (b) The sharp point has a tiny area so the pressure is large enough to pierce the board; the broad head spreads the force over a large area so the pressure on the thumb is small.
items.markingKey: (a) larger area [1]; smaller pressure, less sinking [1] [2] (b) point small area → high pressure [1]; head large area → low pressure on thumb [1] [2]

items.stem: A box exerts a force of 500 N on an area of 0.1 m². Calculate the pressure.
items.markingKey: p = F/A = 500/0.1 = 5000 Pa. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the total pressure on a diver is greater than ρgh. (b) Water spurts from holes at different heights in the side of a tall container. Explain why water from the lowest hole travels furthest.
items.answer: (a) Atmospheric pressure also acts on the water surface, so total pressure = atmospheric pressure + ρgh. (b) The lowest hole is deepest, so the pressure there is greatest and water is pushed out fastest.
items.markingKey: (a) atmospheric pressure adds [1]; p = p_atm + ρgh [1] [2] (b) deepest point [1]; greatest pressure [1] [2]

items.stem: A student studies pressure at the bottom of a column of liquid. The density of the liquid is halved while the depth stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the pressure due to the liquid changes.
items.answer: The pressure due to the liquid halves.
items.markingKey: Using Δp = ρgΔh: pressure due to the liquid ∝ density of the liquid; factor = 0.500 = 0.500. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A point at the bottom of a salt-works brine tank is 2.5 m below the surface of brine (density 1200 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg). Calculate the pressure due to the liquid.
items.markingKey: Δp = ρgΔh = 1200 × 9.8 × 2.5 = 29 400 Pa. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: At a depth of 3 m in oil (density 800 kg/m³), the pressure due to the liquid is p. Calculate the depth in brine (density 1200 kg/m³) at which the liquid pressure is also p.
